title: A physiological subpulmonary ventricle for single-ventricle heart disease

concept.text: The innovation would supply the pumping chamber missing from a Fontan circulation. In children with a functional single ventricle, staged surgery can route systemic venous blood directly to the lungs while the existing ventricle pumps blood to the body. Without a subpulmonary ventricle, blood flow through the lungs depends on elevated venous pressure. A constructed ventricle or actively contracting conduit would add mechanical work between the veins and pulmonary arteries, helping move blood through the lungs without requiring the veins to provide all the driving pressure.

The defining capability is a durable pump that fits pediatric anatomy, supplies appropriate pressure and forward flow, and accommodates years of growth without clinically significant thrombosis, obstruction, or failure. Living muscle and an equivalent mechanical pump are alternative implementations of this capability. A physiological design target discussed in the supplied research is pulsatile pulmonary systolic pressure of about 20–30 mmHg. Required stroke volume depends on how much venous return the device receives: a conduit handling only inferior vena caval flow cannot be treated as pumping the entire volume normally handled by a right ventricle. Valves and pacing can support operation, but neither they nor a passive tube independently provide the missing contractile work.

significance.text: Fontan surgery has made long-term survival possible for many people born with single-ventricle anatomy, but its circulation retains a fundamental physiological burden. Chronic venous hypertension and constrained augmentation of cardiac output contribute to a clinical picture that can include liver disease, lymphatic complications, arrhythmias, and circulatory failure. These are risks and possible outcomes, rather than an inevitable sequence for every survivor. A safe, durable subpulmonary pump could transform care by addressing the missing source of mechanical work underlying passive pulmonary flow.

The most direct potential benefits are reduced venous congestion and improved pulmonary flow and cardiac output. Normal venous pressures, normal output reserve during exercise, and stabilization of established organ disease would each require separate demonstration. Pressure generation alone does not guarantee these outcomes. In the supplied computational study, an inferior vena cava conduit improved hepatic venous pressure and output while increasing superior vena caval pressure. The clinical review also identifies several contributors to impaired exercise capacity, including chronotropic incompetence, arrhythmias, lung disease, skeletal muscle dysfunction, and deconditioning. Restoring pumping work would therefore address an important limitation without necessarily correcting every determinant of functional capacity.

Synthesis: if the pump also accommodated growth and retained its benefit over decades, it could reduce lifelong dependence on passive Fontan physiology. Constructing a whole transplantable heart would remain a further advance requiring capabilities beyond a subpulmonary pump. Creating a missing ventricle before birth shares the physiological objective, but would require a distinct developmental intervention and delivery pathway; success with a postnatal conduit would not establish that prenatal capability.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is sustained, appropriately regulated subpulmonary pumping in a growing child. The device must convert low-pressure venous inflow into useful pulmonary pressure and forward flow while remaining compatible with the available anatomy and the circulation it serves. Producing a pressure pulse in the laboratory is only one component: sufficient stroke volume, effective ejection, and net mechanical work must accompany it. For an inferior vena cava-only design, performance must be evaluated against that pathway’s inflow and its effects on the rest of the Fontan circuit.

For a living conduit, the engineering gap includes achieving much stronger coordinated contraction than the low pressures summarized in the supplied article, maintaining a blood-contacting surface that resists thrombosis, and preserving function as cardiovascular dimensions and demands change throughout childhood. The article identifies anatomical constraints, mechanical failure concerns, and endothelial cells as relevant to preventing thrombus. These are requirements for translation, not demonstrated long-term properties of an implant. An equivalent mechanical implementation would still have to satisfy the defining requirements for pediatric fit, blood compatibility, durability, and growth accommodation.

A further barrier is controlling the entire circulation rather than optimizing one local measurement. The supplied model’s opposing effects on hepatic and superior vena caval pressures show why a pump that benefits one venous territory could worsen another. Appropriate pressure must be interpreted alongside flow, filling conditions, and pulmonary vascular resistance. Successful integration must avoid exchanging one source of congestion for another, and clinical benefit must be assessed against the multiple cardiac and extracardiac causes of Fontan morbidity.

current_state.text: Grewal and colleagues’ 2026 JACC: Advances review, Contemporary Management and Future Directions of Adults Living With a Fontan Circulation, reports that 30-year survival after Fontan approaches 90%, while circulatory failure and multiorgan complications remain major concerns. This documents the substantial achievement of surgical palliation and its continuing physiological limitations. The survival figure is the review’s summary; it should not be read as a universal prognosis for every patient or surgical era.

Emuna, Hu, Marsden, and Humphrey’s 2026 npj Regenerative Medicine article summarizes previously reported tissue-engineered pulsatile conduits as generating maximum pressures of 0.1–0.8 mmHg. It compares that range with approximately 25 mmHg from a healthy right ventricle and discusses pulmonary systolic pressures of 20–30 mmHg as an ideal design target. These quantities establish the scale of the gap described by that article. The experimental range is a historical literature summary, not a verified maximum across the entire field through November 2026, and the physiological target is not an achieved implant result.

The Emuna article’s own work is theoretical and computational. In its patient-specific inferior vena cava conduit simulation, hepatic venous pressure and output improved, but superior vena caval pressure rose from 18.5 to 21.9 mmHg, reported as an 18% increase. This is evidence of a modeled design tradeoff, not a clinical observation. It supports investigating active conduits while demonstrating that useful local pumping does not automatically restore globally normal venous pressures. The supplied evidence does not demonstrate a functioning, durable implanted subpulmonary ventricle.

Unverified research-note claims: the earlier notes attribute an incidence of 2.8 surgically treated univentricular-heart cases per 10,000 live births to a 2024 Swedish study by Dalén and colleagues, DOI 10.1161/JAHA.123.031722. They also attribute stimulated luminal pressure of 1.87 mmHg in a bench conduit to Luo, Qyang, and colleagues in Acta Biomaterialia, DOI 10.1016/j.actbio.2025.06.055, with a February 2026 publication date. Neither source text is supplied, so these numbers, their measurement context, and the publication chronology cannot be verified here. The Swedish estimate concerns surgical cases and should not be generalized to all congenital single-ventricle disease. If confirmed, the attributed bench result would document a limited experimental advance, without establishing durable physiological pumping. The absence of supplied evidence does not show that either result is false.

The supplied review reports access to the full JACC article through retained XML and to the complete 17-page main Emuna article through extracted PDF text. Its conclusions do not include separate supplementary material or inspection of figures beyond the supplied extracted text. The exact 15 January 2026 publication date previously assigned to the Emuna article was not established by that text. The supplied search record is empty, so these dated sources cannot establish an exhaustive account of the field through 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed preclinical demonstration: implant the pump in a large-animal Fontan model and show sustained, physiologically appropriate pulmonary pressure and forward flow, reduced venous pressures across both caval pathways, and increased cardiac output over a prespecified period that includes somatic growth. Measure stroke volume against the venous return actually routed through the device. Pulmonary systolic pressure around 20–30 mmHg is a source-grounded physiological target, but should be interpreted alongside flow, filling pressures, and pulmonary vascular resistance. A laboratory pressure of only a few millimeters of mercury would not satisfy this proposal for restoration of physiological pumping, although it could represent useful intermediate progress. Extensive animal studies before human translation are consistent with the supplied article; this exact protocol is a proposal rather than an established standard.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained physiological pulmonary pumping lowers caval pressures and raises output

completion_criteria.text: Proposed safety and reproducibility requirements: define follow-up duration and acceptable limits for thrombosis, obstruction, mechanical failure, and deterioration of either caval pathway before testing. Demonstrate continued function during growth and changing circulatory demand, rather than relying on a single favorable resting measurement. Independent replication and transparent reporting of anatomy, pump configuration, operating conditions, failures, and adverse effects would make the result convincing. Testing should establish the breadth of anatomy, size, and physiological conditions demonstrated; finite experiments cannot establish universal suitability.
completion_criteria.label: Replicated pump function during growth meets prespecified safety limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration: a cohort of Fontan patients would retain hemodynamic benefit for years, with prespecified evidence that Fontan-associated liver and lymphatic disease stops progressing. Functional capacity, arrhythmia burden, adverse events, and the need for additional interventions should also be followed to determine the practical extent of benefit. Disease stabilization is an ambitious endpoint to test, not an expected consequence already established by the sources. The study should define patient selection and distinguish improvement in congestion from reversal of established tissue injury. These are proposed completion criteria, not consensus thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Years-long hemodynamic benefit accompanies stabilized Fontan-associated liver and lymphatic disease

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: PED-01, Physiological extrauterine support through fetal organ maturity, overlaps in supporting immature organs while a child develops, but concerns maintaining fetal physiology outside the uterus. PED-07 concerns supplying missing cardiac pumping work, potentially for years. PED-06, Prenatal correction that lets severe monogenic disease develop normally, overlaps with the possibility of intervention before birth; its defining objective is correction of severe monogenic disease. Prenatal creation of a ventricle is a distinct possible route toward PED-07’s physiological objective and is not demonstrated by either roster title.

Roster-based synthesis: PED-08, Restoration of nephron endowment after the nephrogenic clock stops, shares the ambition of restoring an organ capability that is absent or insufficient. Its central challenge is generating functional nephron endowment, whereas PED-07 requires a growth-compatible source of circulatory work. PED-12, Drug-free donor-specific tolerance for pediatric solid-organ grafts, could be relevant if an implementation involved donor tissue or transplantation, but immune tolerance and functional pump construction are separate capabilities. Constructing an entire transplantable heart would extend beyond this concept’s subpulmonary function.

Roster-based synthesis: PED-03, Reversal of established childhood stunting and its cognitive cost; PED-04, Controlled reopening of developmental critical periods; and PED-09, Post-symptomatic restoration of severe genetic neurodevelopmental disorders, share the broader concern of recovering function after development or disease has created lasting limitations. They do not supply the missing cardiac work addressed here. PED-05, Prevention of cerebral palsy after perinatal brain injury, and PED-11, One-time in vivo correction of severe newborn metabolic disease before irreversible injury, emphasize preventing downstream injury. PED-07 likewise seeks to reduce secondary organ damage, but improvement of its circulation would not itself establish reversal of established liver, lymphatic, or other injury.

Roster-based synthesis: PED-02, Protective adaptive immunity generated by the newborn; PED-10, Function-sparing cure of H3 K27-altered diffuse midline glioma; and PED-13, Drug-free reset of severe pediatric autoimmune disease, address immune protection, cancer eradication, and immune disease reset respectively. Their common ground with PED-07 is durable pediatric benefit while preserving function. Their defining mechanisms and demonstrations remain distinct, and none should be merged with the subpulmonary-pump capability.

change_log.change: Preserved PED-07’s identity and integrated living and mechanical pumps as alternative implementations of the same missing capability.
change_log.reason: The concept is defined by durable restoration of subpulmonary work rather than one fabrication method.

change_log.change: Replaced guaranteed normalization of venous pressure and cardiac-output reserve with conditional benefits and independently testable outcomes.
change_log.reason: The supplied simulation worsened superior vena caval pressure, and the clinical review identifies several independent contributors to impaired exercise capacity.

change_log.change: Qualified stroke-volume requirements for an inferior vena cava-only conduit and added whole-circulation evaluation.
change_log.reason: The modeled conduit receives only part of total venous return; local improvement can coexist with deterioration elsewhere.

change_log.change: Separated historical experimental pressures, physiological design targets, and computational results.
change_log.reason: The reported 0.1–0.8 mmHg range summarizes reviewed experiments, approximately 25 mmHg is a healthy-right-ventricle comparison, and 20–30 mmHg is a design target rather than an implanted achievement.

change_log.change: Added the modeled superior vena caval pressure increase from 18.5 to 21.9 mmHg and identified it explicitly as simulation evidence.
change_log.reason: This quantitative tradeoff materially limits claims of automatic restoration of normal physiology.

change_log.change: Resolved the JACC author attribution to Grewal and colleagues and retained the review’s near-90% 30-year survival summary with scope qualifications.
change_log.reason: The validated review identifies the authors and full article, while the aggregate survival statement does not establish every patient’s prognosis.

change_log.change: Retained the Swedish incidence and attributed Luo bench-pressure result as explicitly unverified research-note claims.
change_log.reason: Their source texts are absent. Qualification preserves potentially useful information without treating it as established or interpreting missing evidence as disproof.

change_log.change: Removed reliance on an exact January publication date and an asserted later-result chronology.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not establish those temporal details.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion criteria to include both caval pathways, safety, growth, independent replication, and defined practical boundaries.
change_log.reason: Pressure generation alone cannot establish durable clinical benefit, and finite demonstrations establish tested breadth rather than universal applicability.

change_log.change: Preserved the supplied review’s extraction limits and lack of an exhaustive freshness search.
change_log.reason: Full main-article text does not substitute for unexamined supplements or figures, and dated evidence cannot establish the complete field as of November 2026.

change_log.change: Clarified prenatal ventricular creation and whole-heart construction, and mapped relevant distinctions across the supplied roster.
change_log.reason: Shared physiological objectives do not make developmental intervention, whole-organ construction, immune tolerance, and pump engineering interchangeable.

unresolved_issues: The Swedish incidence estimate of 2.8 surgical cases per 10,000 live births remains unverified from the supplied material, including its population definition and applicability beyond the studied setting.

The attributed Luo result of 1.87 mmHg requires source verification, including measurement conditions, comparability with earlier conduit pressures, publication date, and chronology. The review’s recommendation to remove it and the Swedish estimate was not adopted literally; both were retained as explicitly unverified claims to preserve the supplied research without inventing confirmation.
The exact publication date of the Emuna article is not established by the supplied extracted text.
No supplied evidence establishes durable implanted performance during growth or multiyear human benefit.
The design changes needed to improve both caval pathways without introducing other hemodynamic costs remain unresolved.
Whether restoring subpulmonary work can stabilize or reverse established liver and lymphatic disease remains a clinical question.
Specific follow-up durations, safety limits, patient-selection criteria, and acceptable intervention burdens for a convincing demonstration remain to be defined.
The empty supplied search record prevents an exhaustive assessment through 1 November 2026; separate supplements and figures were not assessed beyond the review’s stated extraction scope.

brief.title: A lasting lung pump for children missing a heart chamber
possible: Children born with only one working heart pumping chamber could gain a durable pump to move blood through their lungs. Made from living muscle or a mechanical device, it would fit a child’s body and keep working as they grow.
why: Fontan surgery routes blood from the veins directly to the lungs. Without a pumping chamber along that route, raised pressure in the veins drives the flow. Adding a pump could relieve this pressure and increase the blood reaching the lungs and body.

For people living with this circulation, persistent pressure in the veins can contribute to liver damage and problems with the lymphatic system, which drains fluid from tissues. Relieving that burden could reduce lifelong complications.

sources.showed: Their clinical review describes long-term survival after Fontan surgery alongside continuing risks of circulation failure and damage to other organs.
sources.quote: Even under optimal conditions, the Fontan circulation carries inherent physiologic limitations that predispose to cardiac and noncardiac complications.
sources.cited_for: The continuing burden of a circulation that relies on raised venous pressure to move blood through the lungs.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate that an implanted lung pump prevents these complications.

sources.who: Nir Emuna, Zinan Hu, Alison L. Marsden and Jay D. Humphrey
sources.showed: They calculated feasible designs for a contracting tube. A simulation improved pressure in veins draining the liver and increased blood output, but raised pressure in veins returning blood from the upper body.
sources.quote: Parametric exploration of matrix properties and myo ﬁber orientations yields biomechanically feasible designs.
sources.cited_for: Calculations support the pumping concept while exposing a tradeoff between different parts of the circulation.
sources.not_established: The work does not demonstrate a functioning implant or sustained benefit during childhood growth.

shown: Emuna and colleagues have designed a contracting tube using calculations and tested its effects in a computer model based on a patient’s circulation. Their results show why improving blood flow in one region can worsen pressure elsewhere.

Their review of earlier laboratory work found that tubes built from living tissue produced pressures far below those needed. A durable implanted pump that supplies the missing pumping work remains unproven.
missing: A child-sized pump must sustain useful pressure and forward blood flow while lowering venous pressure throughout the circulation.
An implant must keep working during growth without dangerous blood clots, narrowing or mechanical failure.
Human studies must demonstrate lasting circulation benefits and stabilization of liver and lymphatic disease.

milestones.label: Sustained pumping improves circulation during growth
milestones.explanation: A large-animal Fontan study would have to show appropriate lung pressure and flow, lower pressure in veins from both upper and lower body, and greater blood output during growth. This would establish useful pumping in the whole circulation.

milestones.label: Independent studies confirm safe pumping during growth
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to confirm continued pumping during growth and changing demand, within predefined limits for clots, narrowing and failure. This would establish reproducibility and safety beyond a favorable resting measurement.

milestones.label: Lasting human benefit accompanies stabilized organ disease
milestones.explanation: Patients would have to retain improved circulation for years while liver and lymphatic disease stops progressing. This would establish whether sustained pumping also protects organs.

uncertain: The design needed to lower pressure in veins from both the upper and lower body without other circulation costs remains unresolved.
It remains unclear whether restored pumping can stabilize established organ damage or reverse it.
Follow-up duration, acceptable safety limits and patient selection for convincing studies remain to be defined.

page.title: Subpulmonary pumping for the Fontan circulation
page.definition: In a Fontan circulation, veins returning blood from the body connect directly to the pulmonary arteries. An implanted mechanical pump or contracting muscle chamber would add pressure along this route, sustaining flow through the lungs at lower venous pressure as the child grows. Clinical subpulmonary support has been achieved with an implanted venous cannula connected to a pump outside the body.

goal.need: In exercise tests of 411 young people after Fontan surgery, peak oxygen uptake averaged 65% of the value predicted for age and sex. Even when the single ventricle contracts well, high venous pressure can congest the liver. Helping that ventricle eject blood can leave the congestion untreated. Driving venous blood through the lungs could help a child recover enough to receive a donor heart or provide longer-term support. Relieving liver congestion must also preserve drainage from the upper body.

completion.title: An implanted subpulmonary pump sustains circulatory benefit during growth in children with Fontan circulation.
completion.criterion: A prospective clinical study demonstrates that an implanted subpulmonary pump maintains forward pulmonary flow, reduces systemic venous congestion and increases cardiac output in children with Fontan circulation during documented somatic growth. Congestion does not worsen in either caval territory. The study meets its prespecified safety and clinical-benefit endpoints, covering thrombosis, obstruction and pump failure.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; provisional functional test because no published completion threshold covering pediatric pumping during growth was found.
completion.basis: The 2026 research roadmap calls for durable pediatric support that accommodates growth. RegiVe (NCT04782232) is a prospective post-market registry of the EXCOR venous cannula used with a paracorporeal pump. Its primary endpoints include 30-day mortality, major bleeding and device thrombus, and survival to transplantation. Neither the roadmap nor RegiVe defines a clinical success threshold for an implanted pump during measured somatic growth. The duration, amount of growth and acceptable event rates therefore remain unspecified.

milestones.title: A subpulmonary pump meets its specified pressure and flow targets in a mock circulation.
milestones.criterion: In a mock circulatory loop, measure inlet and outlet pressure and outlet flow across the pump's intended operating range. Compare measured performance with the design specifications for its intended patient size and venous connection. For the NHLBI-funded pump supporting both caval veins, the targets are nominal total flow of 3–6 L/min and a usual pressure rise of 1–15 mmHg. A pressure pulse measured inside a contracting conduit alone does not establish forward flow.
milestones.set_by: ISO/TC 150/SC 6, ISO 14708-5:2020, §§6.6.2.4–6.6.2.7, for active implantable circulatory support devices. The numerical example is the target of NHLBI award R43HL180089. The pressure–flow comparison is a functional benchmark for a living pump, whose regulatory classification is product-specific.
milestones.threshold_quote: Data analysis shall be performed to show that the system performance meets the design specifications for the system.

milestones.title: An implanted subpulmonary pump sustains animal circulation through a prespecified endpoint.
milestones.criterion: In an animal model justified for the intended patient population, the implant meets prespecified, measurable support and safety criteria through the study endpoint. Assess thrombosis, hemolysis, organ dysfunction and hemodynamic stability. Use the final device or document and justify differences that could affect interpretation. For a living pump, the pediatric roadmap also calls for longitudinal assessment of integration, function and growth accommodation in an ovine Fontan model.
milestones.set_by: ISO/TC 150/SC 6, ISO 14708-5:2020, sections 6.12.1–6.12.4. The published benchmark concerns active implantable circulatory support devices; formal applicability to a living conduit requires product classification.
milestones.threshold_quote: Performance shall be assessed based on the ability of the device to provide acceptable circulatory support through a pre-specified timepoint.

milestones.title: A subpulmonary pump provides clinical proof of principle and initial safety data in Fontan patients.
milestones.criterion: An authorized early feasibility study in patients with Fontan circulation demonstrates that the investigational subpulmonary pump provides forward pulmonary flow under its intended conditions of use and reports initial clinical safety data under the study protocol. The protocol identifies any concurrent systemic ventricular support so that the subpulmonary pump's contribution can be assessed.
milestones.set_by: US FDA, early feasibility medical-device study guidance issued on 1 October 2013. This is the published device-development stage; the authorization pathway for a living conduit requires product classification.
milestones.threshold_quote: Early feasibility studies may be used to provide proof of principle and initial clinical safety data.

milestones.title: A pivotal study demonstrates clinical benefit and safety of subpulmonary pumping in Fontan patients.
milestones.criterion: An indication-specific pivotal clinical study demonstrates clinically meaningful benefit in the intended Fontan population and meets its prespecified safety and effectiveness success criteria. FDA's published bar requires clinical benefit beyond demonstration of device function. Patient count, follow-up, endpoints and numerical success limits depend on the product-specific protocol.
milestones.set_by: US FDA, Design Considerations for Pivotal Clinical Investigations for Medical Devices, section 7.1, issued on 7 November 2013. This is general device guidance, not a published Fontan-pump protocol or a classification decision for living conduits.
milestones.threshold_quote: The pivotal study should be designed to demonstrate clinical benefit to the specified subject population rather than to simply demonstrate how the device functions.

milestones.title: A stopped rotary Fontan pump preserves passive forward flow with minimal resistance.
milestones.criterion: With the rotor stopped, pass fluid through the pump in the forward direction and measure the pressure drop over the intended flow range. Assess the drop against the design's specified resistance limit. The funded total-caval design calls for minimal resistance during interruption and gives no numerical cutoff.
milestones.set_by: Perfusion Solutions, NHLBI-funded SBIR award R43HL180089, Phase I hydraulic safety objective for its rotary pump.
milestones.threshold_quote: minimal resistance to forward flow should pump rotation be interrupted

milestones.title: A near-final Fontan pump yields preliminary clinical safety and effectiveness data.
milestones.criterion: Where a traditional feasibility study is undertaken, it evaluates a near-final or final pump for its intended Fontan indication and provides preliminary safety and effectiveness information sufficient to plan the pivotal study. FDA allows this stage to proceed without a separate early feasibility study.
milestones.set_by: US FDA, early feasibility medical-device study guidance, section 3, definition of a traditional feasibility study.
milestones.threshold_quote: capture preliminary safety and effectiveness information on a near-final or final device design

not_found: No Fontan-pump completion criterion specifying support duration, growth accommodation and acceptable adverse-event rates was found.
No registered pivotal protocol with numerical safety and effectiveness endpoints for an implanted Fontan cavopulmonary pump was found.
No prospective human study of a living contractile Fontan conduit was found.
No implanted-pump study demonstrating sustained pediatric subpulmonary support through somatic growth was found.

results.finding: An optimized living-muscle Fontan conduit in one patient-specific simulation increased inferior vena cava flow by 48% versus the passive baseline.
results.detail: The model used one-way valves and compared the active conduit with a passive baseline. The NHLBI total-caval targets apply to a different design that supports both caval veins.
results.quote:
IVC
ﬂow increased from 8.4 ml/beat (61% of total ﬂow) to 12.4 ml/beat (69%
of total ﬂow; Supplementary Fig. 7D), re ﬂecting an augmented IVC
return ( + 48%).

results.finding: One dual-inlet cavopulmonary pump prototype achieved its nominal 12.5 mm Hg pressure rise in a bench loop.
results.detail: The pressure head was calculated from outlet total pressure minus the mean of the two inlet total pressures. Total flow was measured upstream of the inlet split and represents outlet flow in the steady loop.
results.quote: The CPAD was designed for a nominal operating point of 4 L/min against a pressure head of 12.5 mm Hg, which was achieved at a rotational speed of approximately 2,500 RPM.

results.finding: One rotary Fontan pump prototype sustained a positive pressure rise above 10 L/min in a mock circulation.
results.detail: Figure 5 plots measured pressure–flow curves through 8 L/min. The results text separately reports positive pressure rise above 10 L/min.
results.quote:
The CPAD provided support across a broad range with
maintained pressure step-up ’s at high ﬂow rates (Q > 10 L/min
for n > 3200 rpm) and peak pressure heads of 52.68 mm Hg
(Q = 0 L/min, n = 3900 rpm).

results.finding: One stalled rotary Fontan pump prototype passed passive forward flow with a maximum reported pressure drop of 6.3 mm Hg.
results.detail: The paper describes the measured resistance as a trade-off with efficient powered operation and leaves the acceptable resistance during pump failure unresolved.
results.quote:
Pressure losses across the CPAD (light green line, Fig. 5 )i n
case of pump failure (n = 0 rpm, pump stalled) ranged from
0.31 to 6.3 mm Hg with resistances between 0.63 and
3.15 mm Hg/(L/min) (Wood Units) for ﬂow rates within 1 to
4 L/min.

results.finding: Tissue-engineered pulsatile conduits (3 independent batches) generated a mean luminal pressure pulse of 1.87 mmHg under electrical pacing.
results.detail: A single catheter beneath the contracting tissue measured the pressure change over one beat. Forward flow remains unverified.
results.quote: Importantly, at 2 Hz, the luminal pressure developed by TEPCs reached 1.87±0.33 mmHg, which doubles the pressure produced by our first-generation TEPCs at the same frequency

results.finding: Living porcine cavoatrial conduits (total n unreported) generated a mean ex vivo pulse pressure of 9.2 mm Hg.
results.detail: The authors proposed pressure ranges for initial Fontan surgery and failing Fontan physiology as hypotheses. The bench study did not test those ranges as performance targets.
results.quote: The overall mean generated pulse pressure (paced and unpaced) was 9.2 mm Hg.

results.finding: In a five-sheep study, three animals received mini-FCAD support through the planned 30-day endpoint.
results.detail: The sheep received postoperative unfractionated heparin targeting thromboelastography R times twice normal. The text does not identify the complications that ended two studies early.
results.quote: In the final three studies, the animals remained healthy and were electively terminated at 30 ± 2 days.

results.finding: Of 28 reported living muscle grafts implanted in the mouse IVC, 24 contracted synchronously at explant.
results.detail: The abstract reports 28 total grafts, while the stiffness-group counts sum to 32. The mouse-scale prototype differs from the intended Fontan conduit, and the abstract gives no justification for extrapolating support from this model to children.
results.quote:
At time of explant, 24 grafts showed
synchronous contractile behavior of the EHT around the collagen conduit in vivo.

results.finding: In five beagles, an implanted skeletal muscle ventricle restored pulmonary flow to 98 ± 23% of the preoperative value during acute testing.
results.detail: Eight weeks of electrical preconditioning preceded connection of the pump to the circulation. The paper explains the right-atrial filling pressure and high-resistance model in relation to clinical use, but reports only brief support after connection.
results.quote:
PA flow は術 前 (右 室 切 除 前) の35%と 著 しい 右 心 不 全
を認 め た が, SMV駆 動 に よ りCVPは 低 下 し, 98±23%
と 術 前 と同程 度 のPA flow が 得 られ た (図4).

results.finding: Among 32 implanted mouse IVC conduits, over 80% of Moderate and Stiff grafts remained patent through follow-up of up to one year.
results.detail: The pressure catheter recorded pressure inside the graft. The abstract does not report a pressure rise across the graft or a direct measurement of forward flow.
results.quote: Over 80% of Moderate and Stiff conduits remained patent up to 12 months.

results.finding: Two adolescents with failing Fontan circulation received EXCOR support. One had 133 uneventful days of isolated subpulmonary support.
results.detail: Both implantations were reported as uneventful. The isolated-support case helps assess the subpulmonary contribution. In the biventricular case, the contribution of each pump cannot be determined from the reported outcomes.
results.quote: After 133 days of uneventful support the boy was successfully transplanted and discharged home.

results.finding: Two adolescents received support with the design-frozen Fontan cannula. One reached transplantation after 133 days of isolated support.
results.detail: Design freeze and CE approval were reported for the cannula, the dedicated component of the EXCOR configuration. The abstract gives individual clinical courses and does not report aggregate study endpoints.
results.quote: After 133 days of uneventful support the boy was successfully transplanted and discharged home.

results.finding: Two stopped Fontan viscous impeller pump prototypes each had a pressure drop below 2 mmHg at 7 L/min in a mock circulatory loop.
results.detail: At 7 L/min, the stopped pump added at most 0.7 mmHg relative to the empty housing. The authors flagged increased pressure loss at simulated exercise flows.
results.quote: The mean pressure gradient at CO = 7 L/min for the stopped VIPs tested in this study is below 2 mmHg.

results.finding: Rotary Fontan pump (one design, specimen count unstated) had a stalled pressure gradient of ≤1 mmHg.
results.detail: The abstract’s wide-range performance statement does not explicitly apply to the stalled condition. The stated design objective is no obstruction during device failure.
results.quote: In the stalled condition (0 RPM), gradient is ≤1 mmHg.

results.finding: Latissimus dorsi pumps (n = 5 dogs on complete right-heart bypass) delivered 1.14 L/min at the reported assessment.
results.detail: The output was measured after 4 hours of continuous complete bypass. The reported maximum bypass duration was 8 hours, with no prespecified completion endpoint stated.
results.quote: Skeletal muscle ventricle output was 1.14 +/- 0.02 l/min, central venous pressure was 13 +/- 1.5 mm Hg, and systemic systolic blood pressure was 95 +/- 9 mm Hg.

definition = "In a Fontan circulation, veins returning blood from the body connect directly to the pulmonary arteries. An implanted mechanical pump or contracting muscle chamber would add pressure along this route, sustaining flow through the lungs at lower venous pressure as the child grows. Clinical subpulmonary support has been achieved with an implanted venous cannula connected to a pump outside the body.". Reason: The definition now identifies where the pump acts, what growth accommodation means and how an implanted pump differs from the closest human use.

goal.need = "In exercise tests of 411 young people after Fontan surgery, peak oxygen uptake averaged 65% of the value predicted for age and sex. Even when the single ventricle contracts well, high venous pressure can congest the liver. Helping that ventricle eject blood can leave the congestion untreated. Driving venous blood through the lungs could help a child recover enough to receive a donor heart or provide longer-term support. Relieving liver congestion must also preserve drainage from the upper body.". Reason: The survival figures give little sense of daily limitation or of what subpulmonary support could change for a child whose systemic ventricle still contracts well.

add statement by Additional Ventures, 2026: "Restore physiologic circulation by introducing a second functional ventricle". Reason: The roadmap explicitly names restoration of the missing pump as a goal and covers both implementations.

add statement by Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand, 2020: "Development of a subpulmonary ventricular assist device, or cavopulmonary assist device, is an attractive concept". Reason: The society's position statement identifies the clinical setting in which it sees a role for developing a cavopulmonary assist device.

edit completion: basis = "The 2026 research roadmap calls for durable pediatric support that accommodates growth. RegiVe (NCT04782232) is a prospective post-market registry of the EXCOR venous cannula used with a paracorporeal pump. Its primary endpoints include 30-day mortality, major bleeding and device thrombus, and survival to transplantation. Neither the roadmap nor RegiVe defines a clinical success threshold for an implanted pump during measured somatic growth. The duration, amount of growth and acceptable event rates therefore remain unspecified."; refs = [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 21, 22, 25]. Reason: The completion basis omits the registered Fontan support study whose endpoints most closely approach the provisional test.
rename case "Living muscle conduits" to "Living muscle pumps". Reason: The living-pump strategy includes engineered pumping chambers as well as tubular conduits.

edit m1: title = "A subpulmonary pump meets its specified pressure and flow targets in a mock circulation."; criterion = "In a mock circulatory loop, measure inlet and outlet pressure and outlet flow across the pump's intended operating range. Compare measured performance with the design specifications for its intended patient size and venous connection. For the NHLBI-funded pump supporting both caval veins, the targets are nominal total flow of 3\u20136 L/min and a usual pressure rise of 1\u201315 mmHg. A pressure pulse measured inside a contracting conduit alone does not establish forward flow."; set_by = "ISO/TC 150/SC 6, ISO 14708-5:2020, \u00a7\u00a76.6.2.4\u20136.6.2.7, for active implantable circulatory support devices. The numerical example is the target of NHLBI award R43HL180089. The pressure\u2013flow comparison is a functional benchmark for a living pump, whose regulatory classification is product-specific."; set_by_kind = "standards_body"; threshold_quote = "Data analysis shall be performed to show that the system performance meets the design specifications for the system."; threshold_ref = 6; refs = [6, 5, 10, 12, 26]. Reason: The current title applies one project's total-caval operating range to every design, and the criterion mixes bench results with the test.

add milestone after m1: "A stopped rotary Fontan pump preserves passive forward flow with minimal resistance.". Reason: Powered pressure–flow testing misses the separate hazard of a stopped rotor obstructing the child's passive route to the lungs.

edit m2: criterion = "In an animal model justified for the intended patient population, the implant meets prespecified, measurable support and safety criteria through the study endpoint. Assess thrombosis, hemolysis, organ dysfunction and hemodynamic stability. Use the final device or document and justify differences that could affect interpretation. For a living pump, the pediatric roadmap also calls for longitudinal assessment of integration, function and growth accommodation in an ovine Fontan model."; refs = [6, 13, 17, 22]. Reason: The animal criterion currently embeds one sheep's outcome and omits the standard's requirements for the animal model and the version of the implant tested.

edit m3: criterion = "An authorized early feasibility study in patients with Fontan circulation demonstrates that the investigational subpulmonary pump provides forward pulmonary flow under its intended conditions of use and reports initial clinical safety data under the study protocol. The protocol identifies any concurrent systemic ventricular support so that the subpulmonary pump's contribution can be assessed."; refs = [7, 14, 21, 25]. Reason: The early feasibility criterion currently includes a case outcome and leaves unclear which component must provide the clinical proof of principle.

add milestone after m3: "A near-final Fontan pump yields preliminary clinical safety and effectiveness data.". Reason: FDA distinguishes preliminary effectiveness testing of a near-final design from early proof of principle and pivotal testing.
